title: A Simple, End-of-Week Reflective Writing Activity for Secondary Students
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart profiles a simple classroom strategy shared by middle school teacher Teri Cook: having students fold a page into four quadrants and respond to four prompts at the end of each week. The four questions — what worked, what didn't, how can the teacher help, and what are you doing tomorrow — accomplish multiple pedagogical goals simultaneously within a few minutes of class time. Stuart unpacks five reasons the activity is strategically rich: it elicits provisional writing, builds effort-and-efficacy self-reflection, signals teacher availability, creates space for both academic and personal student voice, and provides the teacher with timely formative information about student state. He adds a practical caveat about managing response volume across multiple class periods, recommending staggered reading rather than formal grading. The article models how simple, repeatable classroom rituals can carry substantial motivational and relational weight.
points: The four-quadrant end-of-week reflection drives provisional writing, effort/efficacy self-assessment, and student-teacher connection all in one brief activity that requires no materials beyond a sheet of paper.
Prompt three — 'How can I help?' — signals teacher availability and care, functioning as a quiet Credibility and Belonging cue embedded in a writing task.
The fourth prompt about non-academic life (what are you doing tomorrow) supports Belonging by acknowledging the whole student, not just the academic performer.
In a multi-period setting, the volume of submissions can be managed by reading each class's responses while the next class writes — treating the activity as formative scanning, not grading.
Such end-of-week reflection is good developmental practice for secondary students because it cultivates the habit of pointing one's mind toward specific efforts and the outcomes they produced.
quotes: It gets students reflecting on how the week went, which is right in line with Strategy #8 in The Will to Learn, Unpack Outcomes, Good or Bad.

such reflection is excellent practice for the development of the Effort and Efficacy beliefs, as students have to point their mind towards: A) What they did in the past week (i.e., their specific efforts and lack of efforts). B) What kind of results that produced.
Secondary students don't get nearly as much time for this in school as they need.
It allows students to think and write about both their academic (prompts 1-3) and non-academic (prompt 4) lives, which is great for Belonging.
It provides the teacher with lots of insight into how students are doing in terms of goal clarity, application of effort, motivation, need for assistance, and even at home.

since it's provisional writing (bottom of the Pyramid of Writing), I'd not be closely reading these or grading them but rather looking for anything concerning or noteworthy. The information I'd glean would be great soil for next week's moments of genuine connection (MGCs), Woodenization attempts, and so on.
